section.heading: 4.3. What Derivatives Tell Us about the Shape of a Graph
section.paragraph: Many of the applications of calculus depend on our ability to deduce facts about a function $$f$$ from information concerning its derivatives. Because $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ represents the slope of the curve $$y = f(x)$$ at the point $$\left( {x,f(x)} \right)$$ , it tells us the direction in which the curve proceeds at each point. So it is reasonable to expect that information about $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ will provide us with information about $$f(x)$$ .
section.heading: What Does f ′ Say about f ?
section.paragraph: To see how the derivative of $$f$$ can tell us where a function is increasing or decreasing, look at Figure 1. (Increasing functions and decreasing functions were defined in Section 1.1.) Between $$A$$ and $$B$$ and between $$C$$ and $$D$$ , the tangent lines have positive slope and so $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ . Between $$B$$ and $$C$$ , the tangent lines have negative slope and so $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ . Thus it appears that $$f$$ increases when $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is positive and decreases when $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is negative. To prove that this is always the case, we use the Mean Value Theorem.

The curve begins at a labeled point A in the first quadrant, goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point labeled B, then goes down and to the right, now concave up, reaches its low point labeled C, and then goes up and to the right, and ends at a labeled point D. list.item: (a) If $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ on an interval, then $$f$$ is increasing on that interval.
(b) If $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ on an interval, then $$f$$ is decreasing on that interval.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find where the function $$f(x) = 3x^{4} - 4x^{3} - 12x^{2} + 5$$ is increasing and where it is decreasing.
Solution We start by differentiating $$f$$ :
$$f^{\prime}(x) = 12x^{3} - 12x^{2} - 24x = 12x\left( {x - 2} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right)$$

To use the I/D Test we have to know where $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ and where $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ . To solve these inequalities we first find where $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ , namely at $$x = 0,2,{and} - 1$$ . These are the critical numbers of $$f$$ , and they divide the domain into four intervals (see the number line Figure 2). Within each interval, $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ must be always positive or always negative. (See Examples 3 and 4 in Appendix A.) We can determine which is the case for each interval from the signs of the three factors of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , namely, $$12x$$ , $$x - 2$$ , and $$x + 1$$ as shown in the following chart. A plus sign indicates that the given expression is positive, and a minus sign indicates that it is negative. The last column of the chart gives the conclusion based on the I/D Test. For instance, $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for $$0 < x < 2$$ , so $$f$$ is decreasing on $$(0,2)$$ . (It would also be true to say that $$f$$ is decreasing on the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ .)

section.heading: The First Derivative Test
section.paragraph: Recall from Section 4.1 that if $$f$$ has a local maximum or minimum at $$c$$ , then $$c$$ must be a critical number of $$f$$ (by Fermat’s Theorem), but not every critical number gives rise to a maximum or a minimum. We therefore need a test that will tell us whether or not $$f$$ has a local maximum or minimum at a critical number.

You can see from Figure 3 that $$f(0) = 5$$ is a local maximum value of $$f$$ because $$f$$ increases on $$\left( {- 1,0} \right)$$ and decreases on $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ . Or, in terms of derivatives, $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ for $$- 1 < x < 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for $$0 < x < 2$$ . In other words, the sign of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$0$$ . This observation is the basis of the following test.

note.title: The First Derivative Test
note.heading: The First Derivative Test
note.paragraph: Suppose that $$c$$ is a critical number of a continuous function $$f$$ .

list.item: (a) If $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from positive to negative at $$c$$ , then $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$c$$ .
(b) If $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$c$$ , then $$f$$ has a local minimum at $$c$$ .
(c) If $$f^{\prime}$$ is positive to the left and right of $$c$$ , or negative to the left and right of $$c$$ , then $$f$$ has no local maximum or minimum at $$c$$ .

section.paragraph: The First Derivative Test is a consequence of the I/D Test. In part (a), for instance, because the sign of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$c$$ , $$f$$ is increasing to the left of $$c$$ and decreasing to the right of $$c$$ . It follows that $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$c$$ .
It is easy to remember the First Derivative Test by visualizing diagrams such as those in Figure 4.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find the local minimum and maximum values of the function $$f$$ in Example 1.

Solution From the chart in the solution to Example 1 we see that $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from negative to positive at $$- 1$$ , so $$f\left( {- 1} \right) = 0$$ is a local minimum value by the First Derivative Test. Similarly, $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$2$$ , so $$f(2) = - 27$$ is also a local minimum value. As noted previously, $$f(0) = 5$$ is a local maximum value because $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$0$$ .

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the local maximum and minimum values of the function
$${g(x) = x + 2\sin x} {0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi}$$
Solution As in Example 1, we start by finding the critical numbers. The derivative is
$$g^{\prime}(x) = 1 + 2\cos x$$

so $$g^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$\cos x = - \frac{1}{2}$$ . The solutions of this equation are $$2\pi \slash 3$$ and $$4\pi \slash 3$$ . Because $$g$$ is differentiable everywhere, the only critical numbers are $$2\pi \slash 3$$ and $$4\pi \slash 3$$ . We split the domain into intervals according to the critical numbers. Within each interval, $$g^{\prime}(x)$$ is either always positive or always negative and so we analyze $$g$$ in the following chart.

The $$+$$ signs in the chart come from the fact that $$g^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ when $$\cos x > - \frac{1}{2}$$ . From the graph of $$y = \cos x$$ , this is true in the indicated intervals. Alternatively, we can choose a test value within each interval and check the sign of $$g^{\prime}(x)$$ using that value.
Because $$g^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from positive to negative at $$2\pi \slash 3$$ , the First Derivative Test tells us that there is a local maximum at $$2\pi \slash 3$$ and the local maximum value is
$$g\left( {2\pi \slash 3} \right) = \frac{2\pi}{3} + 2\sin\frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3} + 2\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) = \frac{2\pi}{3} + \sqrt{3} \approx 3.83$$
Likewise, $$g^{\prime}(x)$$ changes from negative to positive at $$4\pi \slash 3$$ and so
$$g\left( {4\pi \slash 3} \right) = \frac{4\pi}{3} + 2\sin\frac{4\pi}{3} = \frac{4\pi}{3} + 2\left( {- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \right) = \frac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3} \approx 2.46$$
is a local minimum value. The graph of $$g$$ in Figure 5 supports our conclusion.

section.heading: What Does f ″ Say about f ?
section.paragraph: Figure 6 shows the graphs of two increasing functions on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ . Both graphs join point $$A$$ to point $$B$$ but they look different because they bend in different directions. How can we distinguish between these two types of behavior?

In part (a) the curve lies above the tangents and $$f$$ is called concave upward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ . In part (b) the curve lies below the tangents and $$g$$ is called concave downward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: If the graph of $$f$$ lies above all of its tangents on an interval $$I$$ , then $$f$$ is called concave upward on $$I$$ . If the graph of $$f$$ lies below all of its tangents on $$I$$ , then $$f$$ is called concave downward on $$I$$ .

note.title: Notation
note.heading: Notation
note.paragraph: We use the abbreviation CU for concave upward and CD for concave downward.

section.paragraph: Figure 8 shows the graph of a function that is concave upward (CU) on the intervals $$\left( {b,c} \right)$$ , $$\left( {d,e} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {e,p} \right)$$ and concave downward (CD) on the intervals $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , $$\left( {c,d} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {p,q} \right)$$ .

The curve begins at x = a, goes up and to the right, bends up like an arch, reaches its high point to the left of x = b, and then goes down and to the right. After the curve passes through x = b, it bends down and reaches its low point between x = b and x = c. It then rises through x = c, bends up, reaches its sharp high point at x = d, then bends down, reaches its low point to the right of x = d, then gradually goes up and to the right to a sharp high point at x = e. The part of the curve from x = a to x = b is labeled concave down; the part of the curve from x = b to x = c is labeled concave up; the part of the curve from x = c to x = d is labeled concave down; the part of the curve from x = d to x = e is labeled concave up; the part of the curve from x = e to x = p is labeled concave up; the part of the curve from x = p to x = q is labeled concave down.

section.paragraph: Let’s see how the second derivative helps determine the intervals of concavity. Looking at Figure 7(a), you can see that, going from left to right, the slope of the tangent increases. This means that the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ is an increasing function and therefore its derivative $$f^{''}$$ is positive. Likewise, in Figure 7(b) the slope of the tangent decreases from left to right, so $$f^{\prime}$$ decreases and therefore $$f^{''}$$ is negative. This reasoning can be reversed and suggests that the following theorem is true. A proof is given in Appendix F with the help of the Mean Value Theorem.

list.item: (a) If $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ on an interval $$I$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward on $$I$$ .
(b) If $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ on an interval $$I$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on $$I$$ .

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Figure 9 shows a population graph for honeybees raised in an apiary. How does the rate of population growth change over time? When is this rate highest? Over what intervals is $$P$$ concave upward or concave downward?

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis t is labeled Time (in weeks) and is displayed from 0 to 18 in increments of 3 units. The vertical axis P is labeled Number of bees (in thousands) and is displayed from 0 to 80 in increments of 20 units. The curve begins at the origin, goes up and to the right, bends downward until the approximate point (12, 38), then rises, now bends upward, exiting the viewing window at approximately (18, 70).

example.paragraph: Solution By looking at the slope of the curve as $$t$$ increases, we see that the rate of growth of the population is initially very small, then gets larger until it reaches a maximum at about $$t = 12$$ weeks, and decreases as the population begins to level off. As the population approaches its maximum value of about $$75,000$$ (called the carrying capacity), the rate of growth, $$P^{\prime}(t)$$ , approaches $$0$$ . The curve appears to be concave upward on $$(0,12)$$ and concave downward on $$(12,18)$$ .

section.paragraph: In Example 4, the population curve changed from concave upward to concave downward at approximately the point $$(12,38,000)$$ . This point is called an inflection point of the curve. The significance of this point is that the rate of population increase has its maximum value there. In general, an inflection point is a point where a curve changes its direction of concavity.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A point $$P$$ on a curve $$y = f(x)$$ is called an inflection point if $$f$$ is continuous there and the curve changes from concave upward to concave downward or from concave downward to concave upward at $$P$$ .

section.paragraph: For instance, in Figure 8, $$B$$ , $$C$$ , $$D$$ , and $$P$$ are the points of inflection. Notice that if a curve has a tangent at a point of inflection, then the curve crosses its tangent there.
In view of the Concavity Test, there is a point of inflection at any point where the function is continuous and the second derivative changes sign.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Sketch a possible graph of a function $$f$$ that satisfies the following conditions:

Solution Condition (i) tells us that $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {- \infty,1} \right)$$ and decreasing on $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ . Condition (ii) says that $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {- \infty, - 2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2,\infty} \right)$$ , and concave downward on $$\left( {- 2,2} \right)$$ . From Condition (iii) we know that the graph of $$f$$ has two horizontal asymptotes: $$y = - 2$$ (to the left) and $$y = 0$$ (to the right).

We first draw the horizontal asymptote $$y = - 2$$ as a dashed line (see Figure 10). We then draw the graph of $$f$$ approaching this asymptote at the far left, increasing to its maximum point at $$x = 1$$ , and decreasing toward the $$x$$ -axis at the far right. We also make sure that the graph has inflection points when $$x = - 2$$ and $$2$$ . Notice that we made the curve bend upward for $$x < - 2$$ and $$x > 2$$ , and bend downward when $$x$$ is between $$- 2$$ and $$2$$ .

section.heading: The Second Derivative Test
section.paragraph: Another application of the second derivative is the following test for identifying local maximum and minimum values. It is a consequence of the Concavity Test, and it serves as an alternative to the First Derivative Test.

list.item: (a) If $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ and $$f^{''}(c) > 0$$ , then $$f$$ has a local minimum at $$c$$ .
(b) If $$f^{\prime}(c) = 0$$ and $$f^{''}(c) < 0$$ , then $$f$$ has a local maximum at $$c$$ .

section.paragraph: For instance, part (a) is true because $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ near $$c$$ and so $$f$$ is concave upward near $$c$$ . This means that the graph of $$f$$ lies above its horizontal tangent at $$c$$ and so $$f$$ has a local minimum at $$c$$ . (See Figure 11.)

image.alt: Details A U-shaped curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed with tick mark c. The curve labeled f enters near the y axis, goes down and to the right, reaches its low point at x = c, and then goes up and to the right. A horizontal tangent is drawn below the curve and touches the curve exactly once at a labeled point P and is labeled f prime (c) = 0. The vertical segment from tick mark c reaches the curve at its low point.

section.paragraph: Note The Second Derivative Test is inconclusive when $$f^{''}(c) = 0$$ . In other words, at such a point there might be a maximum, there might be a minimum, or there might be neither. This test also fails when $$f^{''}(c)$$ does not exist. In such cases the First Derivative Test must be used. In fact, even when both tests apply, the First Derivative Test is often the easier one to use.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Discuss the curve $$y = x^{4} - 4x^{3}$$ with respect to concavity, points of inflection, and local maxima and minima.
Solution If $$f(x) = x^{4} - 4x^{3}$$ , then

To find the critical numbers we set $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ and obtain $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 3$$ . (Note that $$f^{\prime}$$ is a polynomial and hence defined everywhere.) To use the Second Derivative Test we evaluate $$f^{''}$$ at these critical numbers:

Since $$f^{\prime}(3) = 0$$ and $$f^{''}(3) > 0$$ , the Second Derivative Test tells us that $$f(3) = - 27$$ is a local minimum. Because $$f^{''}(0) = 0$$ , the Second Derivative Test gives no information about the critical number $$0$$ . But since $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for $$x < 0$$ and also for $$0 < x < 3$$ , the First Derivative Test tells us that $$f$$ does not have a local maximum or minimum at $$0$$ .
Since $$f^{''}(x) = 0$$ when $$x = 0$$ or $$2$$ , we divide the real line into intervals with these numbers as endpoints and complete the following chart.

The point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ is an inflection point because the curve changes from concave upward to concave downward there. Also $$\left( {2, - 16} \right)$$ is an inflection point because the curve changes from concave downward to concave upward there.
The graph of $$y = x^{4} - 4x^{3}$$ in Figure 12 supports our conclusions.

section.heading: Curve Sketching
section.paragraph: We now use the information we obtain from the first and second derivatives to sketch the graph of a function.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Sketch the graph of the function $$f(x) = x^{2 \slash 3}\left( {6 - x} \right)^{1 \slash 3}$$ .
Solution First note that the domain of $$f$$ is $$\mathbb{R}$$ . Calculation of the first two derivatives gives
$${f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{4 - x}{x^{1 \slash 3}\left( {6 - x} \right)^{2 \slash 3}}} {f^{''}(x) = \frac{- 8}{x^{4 \slash 3}\left( {6 - x} \right)^{5 \slash 3}}}$$
Use the differentiation rules to check these calculations.
Since $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$x = 4$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ does not exist when $$x = 0$$ or $$x = 6$$ , the critical numbers are $$0$$ , $$4$$ , and $$6$$ .

To find the local extreme values we use the First Derivative Test. Since $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from negative to positive at $$0$$ , $$f(0) = 0$$ is a local minimum. Since $$f^{\prime}$$ changes from positive to negative at $$4$$ , $$f(4) = 2^{5 \slash 3}$$ is a local maximum. The sign of $$f^{\prime}$$ does not change at $$6$$ , so there is no minimum or maximum there. (The Second Derivative Test could be used at $$4$$ but not at $$0$$ or $$6$$ because $$f^{''}$$ does not exist at either of these numbers.)

Looking at the expression for $$f^{''}(x)$$ and noting that $$x^{4 \slash 3} \geqslant 0$$ for all $$x$$ , we have $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ for $$x < 0$$ and for $$0 < x < 6$$ and $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ for $$x > 6$$ . So $$f$$ is concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,6} \right)$$ and concave upward on $$\left( {6,\infty} \right)$$ , and the only inflection point is $$\left( {6,0} \right)$$ . Using all of the information we gathered about $$f$$ from its first and second derivatives, we sketch the graph in Figure 13. Note that the curve has vertical tangents at $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {6,0} \right)$$ because $$\left. |{f^{\prime}(x)|}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and as $$\left. x\rightarrow 6 \right.$$ .

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Use the first and second derivatives of $$f(x) = e^{1 \slash x}$$ , together with asymptotes, to sketch its graph.

Solution Notice that the domain of $$f$$ is $$\left\{ x \middle| x \neq 0 \right\}$$ , so we check for vertical asymptotes by computing the left and right limits as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ . As $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ , we know that $$\left. t = 1 \slash x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , so
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}e^{1 \slash x} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}e^{ t} = \infty$$
and this shows that $$x = 0$$ is a vertical asymptote. As $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{-} \right.$$ , we have $$\left. t = 1 \slash x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ , so
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}e^{1 \slash x} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}e^{ t} = 0$$
As $$\left. x\rightarrow \pm \infty \right.$$ , we have $$\left. 1 \slash x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and so
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow \pm \infty}e^{1 \slash x} = e^{0} = 1$$
This shows that $$y = 1$$ is a horizontal asymptote (to both the left and right).
Now let’s compute the derivative. The Chain Rule gives
$$f^{\prime}(x) = - \frac{e^{1 \slash x}}{x^{2}}$$

Since $$e^{1 \slash x} > 0$$ and $$x^{2} > 0$$ for all $$x \neq 0$$ , we have $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ for all $$x \neq 0$$ . Thus $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . There is no critical number, so the function has no local maximum or minimum. So the curve is concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty, - \frac{1}{2}} \right)$$ and concave upward on $$\left( {- \frac{1}{2},0} \right)$$ and on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ .
